transcript:
Meeting: Elmbridge Capital Private VPC Discovery
Recorded: 2026-10-21 14:00 EDT
Duration: ~52 mins
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Ana Duarte (Redwood Solutions), Marcus Hale (Elmbridge CTO), Leah Ortiz (Elmbridge Head of Platform), Sanjay Mehta (Elmbridge Security Eng)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Elmbridge is evaluating Redwood Private (VPC) for inference workloads. Primary concerns: VPC peering/topology, CIDR overlap, region constraints (must be eu-west-1 for some data), private endpoints vs PrivateLink, KMS integration and audit logs, and migration path from current hosted model. Next steps: share architecture doc, SOC2 + ISO, schedule deep-dive bench.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on the account, with Priya our systems engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Marcus Hale: Hi Jordan, good, thanks. Leah, Sanjay here. We're excited to dig in — we got a list of network questions.
[00:18] Leah Ortiz: Yep, we've been through the deck. Main thing for us is the private deployment model, we need it to sit inside our VPCs, no public egress, and certain data processing must remain eu-west-1.
[00:29] Priya Kapoor: Great. I can talk details there — there are a couple of deployment topologies we usually propose: cross-account VPC peering where Redwood deploys nodes in your account, or a customer-managed private control plane with PrivateLink endpoints, or our hosted option with strict egress controls. Each has trade-offs.
[00:45] Sanjay Mehta: On peering — we're worried about CIDR overlap across several business units; we also use Transit Gateway and have some strict route table rules. Can you peer to a transit gateway or do you need direct peering?
[00:58] Priya Kapoor: Good question. We support both. For scale, many customers use Transit Gateway peering — Redwood can accept a TGW attachment from your side to our edge VPC, or we can peer directly if TGW isn't an option. If you want nodes in your account (private nodes), those are deployed into your subnets and no peering is required, but that model has some provisioning overhead.
[01:18] Marcus Hale: Wait — can you clarify \"nodes in our account\" — that would run on our EC2/GPU fleet?
[01:24] Priya Kapoor: We offer two private variants: 1) Redwood-managed Private within your VPC (we deploy our runtime into your account under an MSA/partner onboarding — Redwood maintains the nodes but they live in your VPC), or 2) fully customer-hosted where your infra team spins up the runtime in your environment. Most enterprise customers pick option 1 for easier upgrades and support while keeping network isolation.
[01:45] Leah Ortiz: For regulatory reasons, some workloads must stay in eu-west-1 and never cross to other regions. If Redwood's control plane is in us-east-1, how does that affect data residency?
[01:57] Jordan Lee: Short answer: control plane location is decoupled from data plane. For Private deployments we can pin data plane nodes to eu-west-1, and control plane metadata can be in a separate region with no user data persisted there. We have an architecture doc — we'll share the exact guarantees, but customers often require a private control plane in-region which we can support as part of our Private offering for enterprise deals.
[02:18] Sanjay Mehta: KMS — we require customer-managed keys (CMKs) in our account/HSM for model artifacts and logs. Does Redwood integrate with BYOK?
[02:27] Priya Kapoor: Yes, we integrate with customer-managed KMS keys and support importing a key alias or connecting to an HSM via standard cloud provider integrations. For auditability we can also forward logs to your CloudWatch/Stackdriver and keep audit trails in your account.
[02:40] Marcus Hale: Great. Relatedly, what about Private endpoints — is it VPC endpoints to an S3 bucket for artifacts, or AWS PrivateLink to Redwood control plane endpoints?
[02:50] Priya Kapoor: Both are possible. For artifact storage we typically recommend S3 VPC endpoints with strict bucket policies. For API/control plane traffic we use AWS PrivateLink or interface endpoints so traffic never leaves the AWS backbone. If you prefer, we can use endpoint services so it's cross-account and private.
[03:07] Leah Ortiz: There was a note about NAT gateway egress when nodes fetch model layers — can we avoid public NAT egress?
[03:15] Priya Kapoor: Yes, we can stage model layers into an S3 bucket in your account and have nodes use VPC endpoints to fetch without NAT. Alternatively, if nodes are in our account, we rely on PrivateLink + S3 endpoints in our peered setup to avoid public egress. We'll need to map the flow to decide who owns the S3 buckets.
[03:33] Jordan Lee: High level, Elmbridge has three choices: hosted (fastest), dedicated (reserved capacity in Redwood infra), or private/VPC (the strictest from a network/security standpoint). Looks like you need private.
[03:45] Marcus Hale: Yeah, private is our preference. Questions about SSO and RBAC too — we use Okta SAML and need SCIM provisioning for service accounts.
[03:54] Ana Duarte: We support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning; for service-to-service auth we have mTLS options and short-lived tokens issued via your identity provider. We can map roles to our RBAC model.
[04:05] Sanjay Mehta: Audit logs — we need all inference request metadata (customer id, model id, timestamp) in our log store for compliance. Does Redwood provide that?
[04:14] Priya Kapoor: Yes, Redwood can stream audit logs to your account's log destination. There's a toggle for what metadata is streamed; we can include per-request headers and tokenization metrics if you need. We'll validate with legal what can be exported for PII concerns.
[04:28] [05:00] Speaker 1: (murmur)
[05:05] Marcus Hale: On latency — we have strict 100ms p99 for short prompts across our traders. If nodes are in eu-west-1, will Redwood meet this?
[05:15] Priya Kapoor: Latency depends on model size and sequence lengths. For smaller models like 7-13B optimized and quantized, colocating nodes in eu-west-1 and enabling low-latency placement and local cache/KV results in sub-100ms p99 for short completion workloads in many cases. We'll propose a benchmark plan — microbenchmarks + production-like prompt set.
[05:37] Leah Ortiz: Pricing — what's the rough delta between Dedicated and Private?
[05:42] Jordan Lee: Private tends to have higher one-time onboarding and recurring infra pass-throughs if we deploy into your account. Dedicated (Redwood-managed, isolated capacity) is middle ground: predictable throughput and lower setup friction. We'll put together a TCO comparison.
[05:55] Sanjay Mehta: Network ACLs and security groups — do you need any specific ports open inbound?
[06:02] Priya Kapoor: We'll provide a network checklist. Typically you need outbound HTTPS (443) to Redwood control plane endpoints if using PrivateLink, and internal port ranges for node-to-node communication (we supply the ranges; often ephemeral high ports). For PrivateLink interface endpoints, you only need the interface endpoint ENIs and security group rules.
[06:21] Marcus Hale: We also have cross-account restrictions — everything must be peerable only to specific accounts, and we prefer to avoid sharing subnets. How have others handled that?
[06:30] Priya Kapoor: Two patterns: 1) we use endpoint services (PrivateLink) and customers create interface endpoints in their account — that keeps control, avoids cross-account peering; 2) you can allow our AWS account to create resources via a delegated admin role and we deploy nodes into dedicated subnets that you control. Both meet the security gates; PrivateLink is usually simpler if you want strict cross-account boundaries.
[06:52] Leah Ortiz: Do you support Azure/AKS private networking as well? We have a small portion of infra on Azure in the APAC region.
[07:00] Priya Kapoor: We support Azure private endpoints and AKS deployments for Private option, and GCP with VPC-SC-like patterns. For cross-cloud networking it's more complex, often done via VPN or ExpressRoute/Direct Connect into a transit hub. We can discuss specifics with the infra team.
[07:18] Jordan Lee: Any legal/procurement questions? We can get your security questionnaire filled and share SOC2/ISO docs.
[07:25] Leah Ortiz: Yes, please. Also want to confirm data deletion guarantees and retention windows for logs and model artifacts.
[07:32] Ana Duarte: We support configurable retention and can set automatic purge policies for artifacts; for some deployments we run artifact stores in your account which gives you full control over retention.
[07:45] [08:00] Speaker 2: (typing)
[08:10] Marcus Hale: A couple of nitty-gritty items: CIDR overlap — we've got 10.0.0.0/16 across several BU's and some overlap with vendors. If Redwood needs an isolated VPC, what's the smallest CIDR footprint you require?
[08:22] Priya Kapoor: Minimum depends on expected node count and pod density; typically a /20 gives enough addresses for medium clusters, but we can do smaller if we use ENI-based IP sharing or CNI optimizations. We'll share exact sizing guidance.
[08:36] Sanjay Mehta: What about routing tables — we have strict route propagation rules on TGW, and we require prefix lists for allowed routes. Can Redwood work with prefix lists?
[08:47] Priya Kapoor: Yes, we can accept prefix lists and work with your TGW team. For peering we provide IP ranges in advance and adjust routes accordingly.
[08:58] Marcus Hale: Network egress — we're required to scan all images for vulnerabilities before any node boots. Can Redwood's node images be scanned by our tooling?
[09:07] Priya Kapoor: If nodes are in your account, absolutely. If nodes are in our account we can provide signed images and allow you to run an initial scan during onboarding; we also publish image digests and attestations.
[09:20] Leah Ortiz: Are there logs for per-token costs we can pull for chargeback?
[09:26] Jordan Lee: Yes, Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route/model. For Private you can also stream detailed usage logs to your own analytics endpoints for chargeback.
[09:38] Sanjay Mehta: Any experience with using HSMs for signing model weights or verifying integrity?
[09:45] Priya Kapoor: We can integrate signing workflows with your HSM; model artifact signing and verification is supported as part of the secure artefact pipeline.
[09:54] [10:30] Speaker 3: (crosstalk)
[10:37] Marcus Hale: Ok, last set — deployment timeline and pilot: if we run a 6-week pilot what do you need from us?
[10:45] Priya Kapoor: We'll need CIDR ranges and subnet details, an IAM cross-account role or endpoint setup, sample prompt set for bench, and security requirements. We'll propose a pilot plan: week 1 onboarding and network, week 2 provisioning and baseline bench, weeks 3-4 iterative tests and tuning, week 5 production-like trials, week 6 handoff and recommendations.
[11:05] Jordan Lee: I'll send a draft pilot SOW and the architecture + network checklist. Can we target next Wednesday for the SE deep dive?
[11:12] Leah Ortiz: Works for us. Prefer morning CET, but we'll lock a time.
[11:18] Marcus Hale: Also please include the SOC2 report and any model evaluation docs you have.
[11:24] Jordan Lee: Absolutely. We'll share the security pack and a pricing ballpark for Dedicated vs Private with estimated TCO.
[11:30] Sanjay Mehta: One more — do you have a recommended pattern for automated failover if a region goes down? We use multi-region active-passive.
[11:38] Priya Kapoor: We support cross-region failover via model replication and traffic routing policies. For strict in-region residency we can provide a cold standby in another region but that usually requires contractual constraints. We'll include options in the architecture doc.
[11:50] [12:00] Ana Duarte: Quick note — we sometimes see transcription of product names get garbled, so apologies if any of the labels later look off in the notes.
[12:08] Jordan Lee: Great. Any final questions?
[12:11] Leah Ortiz: No, that's it for now. Thanks everyone.
[12:14] Jordan Lee: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the docs and set the deep dive.
